set.hook: The elBulli trio's three-star lab on Villarroel, World's Best Restaurant 2024, about 30 courses a night.
set.why: Oriol Castro, Eduard Xatruch and Mateu Casañas were elBulli's creative team until 2011, opened Compartir in Cadaqués in 2012, then Disfrutar in Barcelona in 2014. The 2026 MICHELIN guide kept its three stars, and its Classic menu still carries the dish MICHELIN singles out: a multi-spherical pesto with smoked eel and pistachio, built on the spherification technique worked out in the elBulli kitchen. The caviar panchino, a fried bun split and filled at the table, dates from 2016.

set.hook: Berasategui's Barcelona three-star in the Monument Hotel, run at the pass by Veneto-born Paolo Casagrande.

set.hook: Albert Adrià's last Barcelona room: about 25 courses through six linked spaces, two stars since Nov 2025.
set.why: Albert Adrià, elBulli's pastry chief and World's Best Pastry Chef in 2015, opened Enigma in 2017 and kept it when the pandemic closed Tickets and the rest of his group. set.hook: Albert Raurich's Raval counter: Spanish tapas logic through a Japanese lens, behind a walk-in sake bar.

set.hook: Self-taught Jordi Artal's two-star Catalan tasting room on Entença, run with his sister since 2004.
set.why: Jordi Artal, Canadian-born to Catalan parents, left a Silicon Valley tech career and opened Cinc Sentits in 2004 with his sister Amèlia running the room and the wine. He never went to culinary school. The first MICHELIN star came in 2008 and the second at the end of 2020. Time Out describes the precision that followed: a sweet potato roasted for an hour, two quail eggs cooked for exactly 100 seconds. Each meal opens with a layered maple shot that recalls his Canadian childhood.

set.hook: Catalonia's oldest dining room, founded 1786 as a chocolate shop, still serving canelons and duck with prunes.
set.why: Can Culleretes began in 1786 selling hot chocolate and pastries off Carrer de Quintana; the Regàs family bought it in 1890 and turned it toward meals, and the Agut-Manubens family took over in 1958. Sisters Montse and Alícia Agut co-own it now. The house canelons date from the 1950s, and on a Sunday the kitchen can send out 300 of them. Only Madrid's Botín is older in Spain.

set.hook: An 1836 café under the Xifré arcades, a restaurant since 1929, known for shell-free arròs Parellada.
set.why: Josep Xifré opened the Cafè de les 7 Portes in 1836 in his arcaded block facing the port; it became a full restaurant in 1929 and has been run by the Solé Parellada family since 1980. The Parellada rice takes its name from Juli Parellada, a regular who wanted his rice with every shell already lifted out. The house still lists more than a dozen rices and close to 80 dishes, and its 2026 group menus put the Parellada first.

set.hook: The 1897 Casa Martí café where Picasso first showed his work, back to Catalan cooking under the Ferré family.
set.why: Els Quatre Gats opened in 1897 in Puig i Cadafalch's Casa Martí as the meeting room of Rusiñol, Casas and Utrillo; Gaudí, Granados and Albéniz came through, and the young Picasso hung his first solo show here and drew the menu cover. In July 2026 owner Sílvia Ferré told Ara that the family, prompted by the pandemic, had gone back to their father's Catalan cooking: pig's trotters and broths returned to a menu that had dropped them for tourists.

creme.title: Four houses, three stars each
creme.story: Barcelona went into the 2026 MICHELIN guide with four three-star kitchens and came out with the same four; no new third star was given anywhere in Spain. Three are in this lane. Lasarte, in the Monument Hotel, was the city's first, in 2017, cooked by Paolo Casagrande under Martín Berasategui's name. Cocina Hermanos Torres took its third in November 2022 and seats diners around the cooking stations in Les Corts. Disfrutar, opened in 2014 by three former elBulli chefs, added its third in 2023 and was voted the World's Best Restaurant in 2024. The fourth, ABaC, sits uptown and is outside this guide.
creme.where: Disfrutar on Carrer de Villarroel; Cocina Hermanos Torres on Carrer del Taquígraf Serra; Lasarte on Carrer de Mallorca

elbulli.title: After elBulli closed
elbulli.story: When elBulli shut in 2011, its cooks scattered across Barcelona, and several of their rooms are still here. Albert Adrià, the pastry chief, kept only Enigma after the pandemic took his other restaurants; it won a second star in November 2025. Albert Raurich, head chef until 2007, opened Dos Palillos in the Raval in 2008, a counter cooking Spanish ideas through Japan, and in 2026 the Repsol Guide gave it a second Sun. Toni Romero, who worked the meat line to the last service, opened Suculent on the Rambla del Raval in 2012, where the marrow-bone tartare has stayed on the menu ever since.
elbulli.where: Enigma on Carrer de Sepúlveda; Dos Palillos on Carrer d'Elisabets; Suculent on Rambla del Raval

two-stars.title: Two stars, three accents
two-stars.story: Barcelona has five two-star restaurants after the 2026 guide, and three of them are here, each with a different accent. Mont Bar on Diputació still works as a bar: MICHELIN notes an a la carte that asks for three snacks and two mains, and the second star came in November 2025. Aleia, upstairs in Casa Fuster, is cooked by Jerez-born Rafa de Bedoya, who puts Cádiz piriñaca under Palamós prawns; its second star came the same night. Cinc Sentits on Entença has held two since the end of 2020, run by self-taught Jordi Artal and his sister since 2004.
two-stars.where: Mont Bar on Carrer de la Diputació; Aleia on Passeig de Gràcia; Cinc Sentits on Carrer d'Entença

rising.title: The class of 2026
rising.story: The November 2025 MICHELIN gala gave Catalonia only two new one-stars, both in Barcelona, and one went to Kamikaze, a 28-seat room on Rosselló that opened in 2022 as a vermouth bar and now serves Japanese-Mediterranean tasting menus from about EUR 75. The same guide added new Bib Gourmands in the city, among them Glug, a long-bar wine canteen run by two chefs opposite the Sant Jordi pool, open since June 2024, and Oníric, a six-table room in Gràcia whose menus run from EUR 18 to 36 depending on the sitting. All three are run by cooks who trained in the city's starred kitchens.
rising.where: Kamikaze on Carrer del Rosselló; Glug on Carrer de Viladomat; Oníric on Carrer de Rabassa

houses.title: Old rooms, dated menus
houses.story: Barcelona's oldest tables are dated by their founding years more than their cooking. Can Culleretes started in 1786 as a chocolate house off the Rambla, has been with the Agut-Manubens family since 1958, and serves its canelons, made since the 1950s, at a set lunch of about EUR 22. 7 Portes opened as a café in 1836 under the Xifré arcades, became a restaurant in 1929, and still seats diners across its salons; the shell-free rice is named for a regular, Juli Parellada. Els Quatre Gats, opened in 1897, gave Picasso his first solo show, and in 2026 its owners brought back pig's trotters and broths.
houses.where: Can Culleretes on Carrer de Quintana; 7 Portes on Passeig d'Isabel II; Els Quatre Gats on Carrer de Montsió
